a.evidence: Reading down the middle column: ridge cap, then a long tiled roof slope seen from above with a dormer, then a bright cream eave edge at rows 56-57, then a dark shadow row at 58-59 under the eave, then the vertical plank wall with the door. style.evidence: The roof tiles carry cream, orange, light red, mid red, dark red and deep maroon, with a per-tile highlight and scallop pattern comparable to the references. The door's pale frame and the wall are somewhat cleaner and flatter than the references' timber and stone detail, so density is slightly lower, but still acceptable beside them.

a.evidence: Down the middle column there is a long, tiled roof slope with a ridge cap, then a cream eave line at rows 56-57. The door and windows have dark inset frames, and the dormer has its own small roof slope. There is no receding side face.

style.evidence: The roof has per-tile scallops in about 5 red-orange steps, a lit ridge and eave, and a lit dormer window, which is comparable to the reference roofs. The wall and door areas are less textured than the reference walls, but there are no large flat fills, so it is acceptable next to the reference.

a.evidence: Reading down the middle column: the ridge cap, then the tile slope (rows 9-55), then a cream eave line (rows 56-57), then a dark eave shadow (rows 58-60), then the plank wall and door down to a stone base at rows 89-93. This matches how the reference roofs read as top surfaces above their walls.

style.evidence: The roof tiles have 4-5 tones and a regular scallop pattern, but it is a repeated stamp with no per-tile variation and no clumping. The wall is only 3-4 tones of vertical stripes. The door bracing and window frames are flat light-grey lines on red. The stone base is a flat grey band with little shading, unlike the reference stones shaded one by one. A thick near-black outline runs around the whole roof, door and building, which gives a sticker look beside the reference's tinted, selective outlines. Overall it is flatter and more uniform than the references.

a.evidence: Down the middle column: the cream ridge cap is at rows 6-8. Below it comes the tile roof slope, which is many rows tall with per-tile highlights and a dormer. A cream front-edge line sits at rows 56-57, with a dark eave shadow at rows 58-60. Then comes the vertical plank wall with the door and windows in dark frames, and a stone base. The roof is a clearly visible top surface and the wall a distinct front face, matching how the reference building roofs read. No receding side faces.

style.evidence: The roof is well textured, with 5 tones and scalloped per-tile highlights. The wall is thinner: vertical planks with only 2-3 reds, and large flat light-grey door braces and trim. The door panels and the dormer face are fairly flat. A heavy, uniform near-black outline runs around the whole building, roof, door and windows, which gives it a sticker look next to the reference. The reference uses material-toned dark edges selectively. Overall it is a little thinner and flatter than the reference.

a.evidence: Reading a column through the middle: the dark ridge edge, cream highlight row, then many rows of scalloped roof tiles, ending at a lighter orange eave row. Directly under it is a dark shadow band (rows 54-56), then the plaster and door front face from row ~57 to 89. The roof is a large visible sloped surface with a distinct front edge and eave shadow, and the wall is a separate vertical face with an inset door and window frames. This is the same structure as the Beodeul house references.

style.evidence: The roof has about 5 tone steps (cream highlight, light orange, orange, maroon, dark purple) with per-tile scallops. The plaster has speckle dots. The timber is shaded in several browns, with a patterned door, small windows and a flower box. The outlines are dark brown or purple, tinted to match the neighbouring material, and are not black stickers. The stone base is grey with variation. Detail and density match the reference houses.

a.evidence: In the middle column the roof slope (rows 0-53) reads as a tiled top surface. It ends in a lighter tile row at rows 49-53, then a dark eave shadow at rows 54-56, then the wall face (rows 57-89). The wall carries inset door and window frames, timber posts, window sills and a stone base. The structure matches the Beodeul house references, where the roof slope sits above the front wall. The dormer has its own roof edge and dark underside.

style.evidence: The roof has about 5 steps (cream highlight, orange, light orange, maroon, deep purple) with per-tile highlights, as in the reference. The roof tile pattern is very regular and the plaster areas are large and speckled but simple, so it is slightly less rich than the references. It would still sit acceptably next to them.

a.evidence: A single column through the middle reads as a ridge row, then about 50 rows of tiled roof slope. The roof is a clear sloped surface above a separate front face, as in the reference houses, so this is not a front elevation with a thin hat. No receding side faces are drawn.

style.evidence: The roof carries about 5 tile tones (cream highlight, orange, mid, red-brown, dark purple) with per-tile highlights, comparable to the references. a.evidence: The roof is a big visible sloped surface, as in the Beodeul house references. No receding side faces are drawn.

style.evidence: The roof has per-tile scallops in 4-5 steps (cream, light orange, orange, maroon, deep purple). Outlines are dark brown or purple tinted to the neighbouring material, not neutral black. It is comparable in richness to the references, and its flat fills are small.

a.evidence: The roof is a large slope that overhangs the wall and is much taller than a thin rim. It ends in a darker lower band and a dark eave line at rows 20-21 that shades the wall below. The roof is drawn with vertical plank lines and has no distinct front-edge highlight, so it is borderline, but both a roof surface and a wall face are clearly present.

style.evidence: The outline is a dark brown tinted to the wood, which matches the reference approach. The material ramps are only about 4 steps (light orange, mid, brown, dark brown). Each tile carries only about 3-5 colours, against the references' rich tile scallops, plaster speckle and stone shading. It reads thinner and flatter than the reference houses.

a.evidence: Reading down the middle column: the lighter roof slope (rows 0-19) is followed by a dark eave band (rows 20-21), then a darker vertical plank wall (rows 22-35). style.evidence: The outline is a dark brown tinted to the wood, which is fine. The materials have only about 4 steps (light, mid, dark, deep). a.evidence: The roof is a large foreshortened slope that spans most of the upper part of the object. It has a dark eave at rows 18-21 that shades the wall below. The roof is the same tone as the wall and reads partly like a plank wall, and there is no crisp front-edge line. The roof-over-wall structure is still clear, so I pass it narrowly.

style.evidence: The outline is a dark brown tone, which is acceptable. The wood ramp has only about 4 steps (light orange, mid, dark brown, deep brown). a.evidence: The roof is drawn as a flat rectangle of vertical planks, like a wall seen face-on, with only a 1-2 px light cap line at the top. style.evidence: The outline is dark brown and follows the wood. There are about 4 brown steps and some plank-gap and grain variation. Next to the references it has no per-tile highlights, plaster speckle or scallop texture. The roof and wall are mostly uniform strips of a few colours, so it is thinner and flatter than the references.

a.evidence: Down the middle column the roof is a tall tiled surface, and the roof edge is marked by a dark eave band at rows 22-23. Below that is a separate log-wall face with its own plank shading. style.evidence: The roof carries about 5 tones (cream, light orange, orange, red-purple, dark purple) in a repeating tile motif. The outlines are dark brown-black with a slight material tint. There are no large single-colour fills, and the tile density is a little below the reference but acceptable.

a.evidence: Down the middle column there is a tall roof surface with a highlighted ridge row and tile texture. A dark eave shadow at rows 22-23 marks where the roof overhangs. Below it is a separate wall with its own shading. The doorway is dark and inset, and the window has a dark frame with a lighter sill. The roof is a large, clearly drawn slope rather than a thin cap, and the wall below is a distinct vertical face, so the building reads as 3/4. Roof slopes count as the top surface for this kind.

style.evidence: The roof has about five steps (dark purple, maroon, orange, light orange, pale yellow) in a dense repeating tile pattern. It is busy and stamp-like but carries texture. The wall has several browns with plank grain and dark bands. Outlines are dark brown, tinted to the material rather than near-black. The silhouette is a plain rectangle and simpler than the gabled references, but the tile information density is comparable. The only large flat area is the dark door, which is small.

a.evidence: Down the middle column there is a tall roof slope (about 19 rows) that reads as a sloped top surface, like the reference roofs. A dark eave band sits directly under it, then the log wall with a darker inset door and window. A lighter horizontal porch ledge at rows 35-37 sits on posts and is a visible horizontal surface. The roof is a flat rectangle with no ridge or hip, but it still reads as a roof surface over a front face, so it passes the 3/4 contract.

style.evidence: The roof has about 5 tones (cream, orange, dark orange, purple, dark purple), but they form a mechanical, evenly repeated stamp pattern with no per-tile variation, and the top row of cream squares looks artificial. The log wall has some grain, but the door is a flat dark block, the porch ledge is a flat band, and the posts are plain. The outlines are dark brown and tinted, which is good. Next to the plaster, stone and timber-frame references, with their hipped roofs and stone shading, this piece is thinner, flatter and more sticker-like in its roof and wall detail.

a.evidence: Reading the column through the door: the roof slope runs from row 2 to 21 and ends in a light orange eave line. Rows 22-23 are a dark eave shadow. The log wall front follows (rows 24-35), with a dark inset door and a framed window with a dark top and left inner edge. A lighter wooden counter band at rows 35-37 sits on legs, so a horizontal surface is visible. The structure follows the same roof-over-wall layout as the Beodeul house references, so the roof reads as the top slope and the wall as the front face. The roof is tall relative to the wall, but it is a legitimate slope surface.

style.evidence: The roof carries 5 or so tones (cream highlight, light orange, orange, magenta, deep purple) in a repeating tile pattern, which is a bit mechanical compared with the reference scalloped tiles. The wall has plank grain, dark bands and a framed window with a lighter lintel. The outline is a dark brown tone at the edges and the doorway is near-black, so it is mixed rather than a sticker outline. There are no large flat fills except the door opening, which is expected. The piece is small and simpler than the references, with slightly lower tile density, but it is acceptable next to them.

a.evidence: Reading one column through a rail, I see a light strip, a dark gap, then a second lighter rail, all drawn face-on. The posts are flat vertical bars with a tiny cap. The rails and the base show no foreshortened horizontal top faces. The side rails are flat strips, and the south fence has no visible top or base surfaces. The interior field is drawn as a flat top-down plan. The frame is therefore a front elevation with small caps, not a 3/4 construction. Strict reading: fail.

style.evidence: The fence wood has about 4-5 brown steps, with a dark brown outline that leans toward the wood rather than neutral black. The wheat is a checker of yellow and ochre dots. The cabbages are shaded in 4 greens with highlights, and the soil and grass tufts carry grain. I see no large flat fills, and tile density is comparable to or higher than the reference. It would sit acceptably next to the stall and well references.

a.evidence: The field, which is the largest volume, is drawn as a top-down plan: crop rows are stacked from above with no south face and no height. The fence posts are flat front-elevation cylinders with a tiny 2-3px cap. The rails are thin horizontal strips with no real top surface, and the side rails are drawn as flat vertical planks. The result is a mix of plan and elevation. No horizontal beam or base shows a foreshortened top over a distinct front face, so it is not a 3/4 frame.

style.evidence: The wood posts have a highlight, light, mid and dark ramp plus grain and knot dots. The crops use 4-5 greens with per-plant highlights. The wheat has dithered speckle in several yellows and ochres, and the soil has grain. Outlines are very dark brown on the wood and dark green on the crops, so they are mostly material-toned but near black in places. Tile density is clearly as high as the reference. The piece has no large flat fills and would sit acceptably next to the Beodeul stall and well.

a.evidence: The largest volume is the planted field, a flat ground patch drawn as a top-down plan with rows of crops and no south face under it. The fence posts have small light caps and the rails read as thin 2-3 px bands over dark gaps. These details are minor next to the field, and the side and rear fences are drawn as flat strips. Overall it reads as a top-down plan with a fence border, not a 3/4 frame whose beams and base show top and front faces.

style.evidence: The wood posts and rails use several brown steps with a light cap and dark brown outlines tinted toward the wood. The wheat is dithered in yellow, gold and cream. The cabbages are shaded in 4-5 greens, and the soil and grass tufts carry grain and variation. There are no large flat fills, and the tile density is as rich as the Beodeul references.

a.evidence: The frame is a fence of posts and rails. Reading a column through a rail at the top gives a light brown rail face, a dark gap, then another rail face. This is a flat elevation with no distinct top band. The post caps are tiny 2-3 row squares and the rails have no visible top faces. The side rails are flat vertical strips with no top or front distinction. The field inside is a flat plan view. The frame's horizontal beams and base do not show top faces, so it fails the contract for a frame.

style.evidence: The outlines are dark brown beside wood, which fits the Beodeul approach, and the crops carry real texture: wheat speckle, cabbage clumps with 3-4 greens, and soil grain. The fence wood is more limited, with about 3-4 steps and long flat bands on the rails and side posts. Overall it is a large tiling field rather than a standing prop, so its density per tile is a little below the reference's, and the fence wood is shallower than the roofed well or stall wood. A careful artist would find it thinner than the reference in the fence portions.

a.evidence: The crop field is a flat map-like plan with no front face or standing volume. The fence posts and rails are drawn in elevation, so no horizontal beam top or base reads as a surface seen from above. It is not an open frame or rack; it is a ground patch with a fence ring. It does not follow the 3/4 contract of a top band plus a front face.

style.evidence: The reference pieces are a stall and a roofed well, standing props, while the candidate is a large fenced crop field, so the kind comparison is only loose. The candidate has rich texture: wheat with highlight flecks, leaf tufts in several greens, shaded cabbages with dark-green undersides, soil grain, and wood rails in 4-5 tan/brown steps. Outlines are dark brown beside wood and dark green beside leaves, so they are tinted rather than black. Tile density is high. It matches the Beodeul craft level, although the pale grey checker ground inside the fence is a plain flat pattern.

a.evidence: The farm is mostly a plan view of crop rows seen from above, filling the interior with no vertical front face. The fence sides are drawn as flat strips. The rails are front-on bands with no distinct top surface and no front-edge line or eave shadow. It is not an open frame or rack with beams and a base showing top faces, so the kind label does not fit and the 3/4 contract is not met.

style.evidence: The wheat has speckled highlights in 4-5 yellows and browns. The cabbages have 4-5 green steps with dark green undersides. The soil rows carry grain and the wooden rails have 4 tones. Outlines are dark brown beside wood and dark green beside leaves, not near-black. No large flat fills, and per-tile colour counts are high, comparable to the reference stall and well.

a.evidence: The main body is the crop plot, drawn as a flat plan seen from above, with rows of plants laid out on a ground plane. It has no front face, no height and no standing structure. The fence rails are thin side elevations and are a minor detail. The piece does not fit the open-frame kind either; it is a flat field tile, not a rack with beams and a base. It is a top-down plan with no front face, so it fails.

style.evidence: The crops carry several greens and golds with per-plant highlights, and the soil has grain. The wood fence is shaded in 3-4 browns with dark-brown outlines, not black. The wheat is speckled with highlights, and the grey ground is dithered, so there are no large flat fills. Tile density is comparable to the references.

a.evidence: The main body is the crop field, which is a flat map-style plan. Its rows are laid out top to bottom as ground coverage, not as a standing volume with a top and a front face. The fence rails are flat tan bands with dark gaps and read as front-facing slats, with no horizontal top surface and no front face below one. Posts are vertical strips with no visible caps. The object is a ground patch with a border rather than a rack or frame, so the kind label fits poorly. It is a top-down plan, so it fails.

style.evidence: The crops use several greens, with shaded cabbages, leaf tufts, wheat speckle in yellows and cream, and furrowed soil grain. The wood fence has light, mid and dark browns, and its outlines are dark brown rather than black. The grey checker ground is broken up with dither, and no large flat fills appear. Each tile carries many colours, comparable to or richer than the reference stall and well.

a.evidence: Terrain ground patch, not a standing object. The 3/4 contract for standing objects does not apply. It reads as a ground autotile block with a top crop strip and tilled soil furrows, with no isometric side faces. Accepted as terrain.

style.evidence: Candidate carries many tones per material: the crop strip has speckled yellows/olives/cream, the grass has 4-5 greens with blade clumps, and the soil has several browns with lighter clods and sprouts. Dark edges are dark brown or dark green, tinted to the adjacent material, not neutral black. There are no large flat fills, and the texture is dense and richer than the reference grass and paving.

a.evidence: The object is a terrain/ground patch, not a standing object. The 3/4 top-and-front contract does not apply to it. It reads as a flat field with crop rows and soil furrows seen from above. It has no standing volume, no side faces and no elevation-style face, so nothing in it breaks the terrain contract.

style.evidence: The yellow crop band is dithered in about 5 tones of gold, olive and cream, with per-pixel speckle. The grass strip has 4-5 greens in blade clumps. The soil has dark, mid and light browns with clod highlights and small green sprouts. The dark outlines lean brown and green, matching the neighbouring material, and are not neutral black. There are no large flat fills, and tile density is at least as high as the Beodeul grass and paving references, which have fewer colours per tile. The piece looks like a coherent, richly textured ground patch.

a.evidence: The candidate is a ground/terrain autotile patch made of horizontal bands of crop, grass and tilled soil. It is not a standing object, so the top-plus-front contract does not apply. Terrain is a valid kind and no receding side faces are drawn. The patch has some pseudo-vertical layering (grass edge over soil) but reads as ground.

style.evidence: The candidate has a lot of per-pixel variation: the golden crop area uses yellow, cream, olive and brown dithering, the grass tufts use 4-5 greens, and the soil uses several browns with lighter clods and sprouts. Dark edges next to the soil are dark brown and next to the grass dark green, so they are tinted by material rather than neutral black. There are no large flat fills. Density is at least equal to the Beodeul grass and paving references, which are comparatively sparse.

a.evidence: This is terrain, so the 3/4 contract for standing objects does not apply. Wheat (rows 0-15), grass (16-21), and furrowed soil with sprout tufts (22-47) all read as ground surface. No isometric side faces and no object elevation are drawn.

style.evidence: Each material has several lightness steps: wheat in cream, yellow, olive and brown; grass in about four to five greens; soil in about four to five browns with lighter clods. Dark edges are tinted dark brown or dark green rather than neutral black. Wheat speckle, grass tufts, furrow grain and sprouts give no large flat fills. a.evidence: The candidate is a flat ground patch of crop rows and soil, not a standing object. The 3/4 top-and-front-face contract does not apply, and no receding side faces or elevation drawing is present. Terrain is judged as ground.

style.evidence: Each material has several tones. The wheat rows use pale cream, bright yellow, orange and ochre-brown speckle. a.evidence: The candidate is a terrain tile block (farm ground), not a standing object, so the 3/4 top-and-front contract does not apply. It is a flat ground surface of crop rows and soil furrows with no side faces and no elevation. Nothing in it conflicts with the terrain kind, so it is judged as ground.

style.evidence: The wheat rows use about 5 yellow/orange/cream steps with per-pixel speckle. a.evidence: Terrain tile set with horizontal bands of crop and soil texture. style.evidence: Wheat uses about 5 tones (cream highlights, yellow, orange, brown). Soil uses 4-5 browns with lighter clods and dark furrows. Crops use 4 greens in clumps with sprout highlights. a.evidence: The kind is terrain (ground), so the standing-object 3/4 contract does not apply. It is a flat ground patch of crop and soil rows with no standing volume, no isometric side faces, and no hat-on-elevation construction. Terrain is accepted as ground.

style.evidence: The wheat uses about 5 yellow and ochre steps with pale highlight flecks. The crops use about 4 greens with lighter tufts. The soil has about 5 browns with lighter clods and grain. style.evidence: The wood has about 4 brown steps with a few grain dots, and the dark outline is brown-tinted, which fits the standard. a.evidence: The largest volume is the left wood rail, which runs about 48 rows as a flat front face with no top surface at all. style.evidence: The wood has about 4 tones (light tan, mid brown, dark brown, near-black gap) with only a little grain. a.evidence: Each post is a narrow vertical shaft with a small tan cap and a flat brown face below it. style.evidence: The wood ramps have about 3-4 steps with some grain. The dark near-black background fills large flat areas, and the grey blocks are flat with 2-3 tones. a.evidence: The posts are drawn as flat vertical grain with no visible top surface. The grey rails are thin 2-row strips with no readable top face and no set-back front. style.evidence: The wood uses about 4 tonal steps with a dark brown, material-tinted outline, which is fine. The wooden frame is fairly flat with only 2-3 browns, and the lower-left area has little grain. The drum body is smooth gradient-banded without much dotting, so it is slightly less rich than the stall and well references, but it would sit acceptably next to them.

a.evidence: Down the middle column: the tan elliptical drumhead (rows 3-12) is a clearly visible horizontal surface with a lighter highlight. Below it a gold stud row marks the front edge at about row 12-13. The orange shell then runs from row 13 to about 21 with a dark red shadow, and a gold-stud band at the bottom. The wooden frame posts and a base beam sit behind and below it. This reads as a correct ellipse-capped cylinder like the green barrel and column in the guide.

style.evidence: The drum body has about 5 orange steps (light left highlight, mid, dark right shadow, deep red) and the drumhead has 3-4 tan steps. Outlines are dark red-brown and brown tinted to the material. The gold studs add detail. The wooden frame is flatter, with only 2-3 browns and little grain, and the lower part of the shell has some smooth gradient areas. Overall it is close to the reference but slightly thinner.

a.evidence: Down the middle column, the roof and pulley come first. Then the light stone back rim (rows ~14-16) and the dark blue water ellipse with a highlight (rows ~17-21) follow. A lighter front rim edge comes next, then the darker block-stone front face (rows ~23-31) with a shaded course. The opening is a real elliptical interior with several rows of height, so the horizontal surface reads clearly from above. There is no receding side face.

style.evidence: The stone has about 5 steps, with a light rim, mid and dark blocks, a deep base and blue water. The outlines are dark tinted tones rather than black. The wooden roof beam is a large flat orange slab (about 30x4 px) with only a highlight line and a dark underside. It has no grain or planks, unlike the roofed reference's tiled, textured roof. The posts are flat single-tone columns. The stone blocks are fairly large smooth fills with little speckle. Overall it is thinner and flatter than the Beodeul well.

a.evidence: A middle column meets the light back rim (rows 14-15), then a dark blue water ellipse with highlights (about rows 16-20). Below it comes a lighter front rim edge (about rows 21-22), then a darker stone-block front face with shaded courses (rows 23-31). The opening is a visible ellipse, and the rim reads as a horizontal surface above a separate vertical face. The guide's ellipse-top examples (column, barrel) look the same way.

style.evidence: The stone has about 5 steps (pale highlight rim, light, mid, dark, deep base), and the blocks are shaded individually. The water has 3 tones with a highlight. The outlines are dark teal-grey and tinted like the adjacent stone, not pure black. The wood roof and posts have 3-4 tones with some grain. The piece is slightly simpler than the roofed reference but has no large flat fills, so it is acceptable next to it.

a.evidence: Down the middle column: the light rim at the back (rows 14-15), then a dark elliptical opening with blue water and a highlight (rows 16-21), then a lighter front lip (rows 21-22). Below that the front face runs from row ~23 to row 31, built from shaded stone blocks. The rim reads as a wide horizontal ring seen from above, and the opening shows its interior, so it matches the guide's ellipse-top examples rather than a flat rim line.

style.evidence: The stone ramp has about 5 steps (pale rim, light, mid, dark, deep), with individually shaded blocks and a water highlight. Outlines lean teal-grey to dark brown rather than being neutral black. The wooden beam and posts are simpler, with 2-3 tones and little grain, and there is no tiled roof like the reference's, so density is a bit below the reference. The stone body carries enough variation to sit acceptably beside it.

a.evidence: In the middle column the rim is light grey (rows 14-16), then an elliptical dark-blue opening with highlights (rows 16-20), then a lighter front rim line (row ~21), then the front wall of shaded stone blocks (rows 22-31). The opening reads as a real ellipse seen from above, with the front wall below it. No isometric side face. The stone blocks are painted rather than inset, but the construction is correct 3/4.

style.evidence: The stone well has about 5 grey-green steps, a tinted dark outline and shaded block faces with a bit of water glint, which is decent. The wooden roof beam and the posts are large flat tan fills with only a highlight row and a shadow row, and no grain. Several stone blocks are also smooth flat patches. The reference well has richer tile and wood texture, so tiles here carry fewer colours and look thinner next to it.

a.evidence: Down the middle column: the light salmon top surface (rows 5-9) is clearly a horizontal plane, about 5 rows deep. Below it a lighter edge step and a darker band of shade lead into the reddish-brown front apron (rows 10-13), which darkens toward the bottom. The dark legs below at rows 13-15 show the piece stands open underneath. The top and front are both clearly drawn, and the top is a real surface, not a rim. The front has no inset details, but the table has none to show, so the edge step and eave shade are enough.

style.evidence: The wood has about 5 tones: light top, mid top, edge highlight, graded apron and dark leg and shadow. The outline is a dark brown tinted to the wood, not black. Texture comes from speckled darker pixels on the top, cream highlights and the banded apron gradient. There are no large single-colour fills. It is somewhat thinner than the richly textured stall and well references, but acceptable next to them.

a.evidence: In a middle column I read a light salmon top about 5 rows tall. A slightly lighter edge row follows, then a clear drop to mid-brown and a dark brown shadow row under the overhang, about 4 rows of front face in all. Below that, short legs sit at the ends with a dark recessed gap between them, so the front reads as set back under the top. The top is a real horizontal surface that holds the bowl and cloths. There is no front drawer or door, so recessed_front is false. That is fine for a low table. No receding side face is drawn.

style.evidence: The wood ramp has about 5 steps: light salmon top, speckle, a lighter edge, mid-brown and a deep brown shadow. The dark edges lean brown rather than neutral black. The top carries speckle and the bowl has its own highlight and shadow. The front face is mostly smooth banded gradients with little grain, so it is a little thinner than the stall and well references. It is still acceptable beside them and has no large flat fills.

a.evidence: The column through the middle shows a light top band (about rows 5-9) with props placed on it, so it reads as a surface seen from above. Below it the apron steps down through progressively darker browns (rows 9-13), and then a dark shadow with legs (rows 13-15) shows the front set back under the top. There is no crisp front-edge highlight, because the transition is a smooth gradient. The top is still several rows deep, clearly lighter than the face, and carries objects, so it is not a rim or a hat on an elevation. It is a borderline but acceptable 3/4 table.

style.evidence: The wood has about 5 tonal steps, with speckle variation on the top and a graduated apron. The outline is a dark brown wood tone rather than black. The front apron is mostly smooth horizontal banding with little grain, and the piece is a bit thinner than the richly detailed stall and well references. It is still acceptable beside them and does not look like a sticker.

a.evidence: In a column through the middle, the light salmon top covers rows 5-9, a slightly lighter or different tone at about row 9-10 marks the front edge, and the darker red-brown apron follows over rows 10-13, ending in a very dark shadow row under the table between the legs. The legs are at rows 13-15. The top is a clearly visible horizontal surface above a distinct front face, so it reads as 3/4. The front has no drawers or doors, so recessed_front is false.

style.evidence: The table has about 4 brown/salmon steps, from the light top through the mid and dark apron down to the shadow, plus a few speckle pixels on the top. Next to the stall and well references it is thinner. The top and apron have fairly large smooth areas with only gradient banding, there is no wood grain, and the legs are simple dark blocks. The outline is mostly value separation with a darker underside, but there is no clear tinted material outline. Overall it is cleaner and flatter than the references, so under the strict standard it fails.

a.evidence: In the middle column, rows 5-8 are a light tan tabletop that reads as a horizontal surface, with grain and a teapot sitting on it. Row 9 is an orange front-edge line, rows 10-11 are a darker red apron that gives the eave shadow, and rows 12-15 are a dark brown under-band with yellow studs and legs. The top is a real band about 4 rows tall, not a rim, and the front face and legs sit below it. The front has no inset details, but the top, edge line and shaded apron make it a 3/4 object.

style.evidence: The ramp runs cream, tan, orange, red, dark red and brown, so about 5 steps. Outlines are dark red-brown and follow the neighbouring material rather than near-black. The top has grain specks and grey spots, and the teapot has its own shading. The red apron is a fairly plain band but only 3 rows tall, so it is not a large flat fill. It is a small piece with slightly lower tile density than the stall and well references, but it is not sticker-like and holds up beside them.

a.evidence: Reading one column down: orange rim at row 5, then tan top surface for about 4 rows (6-8). An orange front-edge line follows, then red apron rows 9-11 with a darker red shadow line under it. Below that, the set-back dark under-shelf with yellow knobs and the legs run to row 14. The top surface is several rows tall and clearly separate from the front face, so this is a 3/4 table, not a rim-only or elevation drawing. The thin left edge is only the table's end rim.

style.evidence: The ramps run tan, light tan, orange, red, dark red and brown, about 5 steps. Outlines are dark red-brown, tinted by the neighbouring wood, not black. The top has a few grey speckles and light/dark tone breaks, and the red apron has a highlight edge. The piece is small and simple next to the stall and well, so it is slightly less dense. No flat fill reaches 5x5 pixels, so it would sit acceptably beside the references.

a.evidence: In the middle column the light tan top surface runs for about 4 rows. An orange front-edge line follows, then a dark red apron band that reads as the overhang shadow. Below that is a darker under-rail with yellow fittings, and the brown legs sit set back beneath it. The top is clearly a horizontal surface above a distinct front face, so it is 3/4 and not a hat on an elevation. The top is a little shallow, but it is more than a rim and it holds the teapot and a tea-set detail.

style.evidence: The ramps are tan, light tan, orange, red, dark red and brown, which is close to the reference's 5-6 steps. Outlines are dark red-brown that follow the wood and are not neutral black. The top has speckle and highlights around the teapot and the red apron has banded tones, so there are no large flat fills. It is a small piece, and its tile density is only slightly below the stall and well. It would sit acceptably next to them.

a.evidence: Reading down the middle column: orange rim at row 5, tan top surface at rows 6-8 (4 rows with cup and plate details), orange front-edge line, then a red apron at rows 9-10 that reads as the eave shadow. Below that is a brown band with yellow handles at row 11 and dark legs set back at rows 12-15. The top is a clearly visible horizontal surface above a distinct front face, and no receding side face is drawn. The front is mostly flat, but the top band, front edge and shadow are all present, so it reads as 3/4.

style.evidence: The wood ramp has cream, tan, orange, red, dark red and brown steps. Outlines are dark red-brown, tinted to match the wood rather than black. The tabletop has grain and prop detail (teapot, grey cups), and there are yellow accents. No area is 5x5 or larger in a single flat colour. It is a small piece and slightly thinner than the large stall and well references, but it would sit acceptably next to them.
